name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLSPHENOLSETHERS_MCQ_Q01 - Mechanism sequence of acid catalysed hydration of alkene

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following mechanistic steps for the acid-catalysed hydration of an alkene to form an alcohol in the correct chronological order:

(1) Deprotonation of the oxonium ion to form the alcohol
(2) Protonation of water by \(\mathrm{H^+}\) to form hydronium ion (\(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\))
(3) Nucleophilic attack of water on the carbocation
(4) Electrophilic attack of \(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\) on the alkene to form a carbocation

Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Acid-catalysed hydration of an alkene proceeds via an electrophilic addition mechanism involving a carbocation intermediate.

Step 2: Chronological Analysis
First, the acid protonates water to generate the active electrophile, the hydronium ion (\(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\)). Second, \(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\) attacks the \(\pi\)-bond of the alkene to form a carbocation intermediate. Third, a water molecule acts as a nucleophile and attacks the positively charged carbocation to form a protonated alcohol (oxonium ion). Finally, deprotonation of this oxonium ion by water yields the neutral alcohol and regenerates \(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence of steps is protonation of water to \(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\), electrophilic attack on the alkene to form a carbocation, nucleophilic attack of water on the carbocation, and deprotonation to give the alcohol, which corresponds to 2 \(\rightarrow\) 4 \(\rightarrow\) 3 \(\rightarrow\) 1.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLSPHENOLSETHERS_MCQ_Q02 - Chronological stages in commercial fermentation of sucrose to ethanol

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following stages involved in the commercial production of ethanol from sucrose by fermentation in the correct chronological order:

(1) Action of zymase on hexose sugars
(2) Hydrolysis of sucrose catalysed by invertase
(3) Formation of ethanol and carbon dioxide
(4) Formation of glucose and fructose (\(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\))

Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fermentation of molasses or cane sugar converts the disaccharide sucrose into ethanol through two sequential enzyme-catalysed reactions.

Step 2: Chronological Analysis
First, sucrose (\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}\)) undergoes hydrolysis in the presence of the enzyme invertase. This produces the monosaccharides glucose and fructose (\(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\)). Next, the enzyme zymase (present in yeast) acts on these hexose sugars under anaerobic conditions. Finally, fermentation is completed with the formation of ethanol (\(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)) and carbon dioxide (\(\mathrm{CO_2}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct order of stages is hydrolysis of sucrose by invertase, formation of glucose and fructose, action of zymase on hexose sugars, and formation of ethanol and carbon dioxide, which corresponds to 2 \(\rightarrow\) 4 \(\rightarrow\) 1 \(\rightarrow\) 3.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLSPHENOLSETHERS_MCQ_Q03 - Industrial synthesis sequence of phenol from cumene

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps for the industrial manufacture of phenol from cumene (isopropylbenzene) in the correct chronological sequence:

(1) Treatment of the hydroperoxide intermediate with dilute acid
(2) Formation of cumene hydroperoxide
(3) Aerial oxidation of cumene with \(\mathrm{O_2}\)
(4) Formation of phenol and acetone

Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Most of the worldwide production of phenol is carried out from cumene via a two-stage oxidation and acid-catalysed cleavage process.

Step 2: Chronological Analysis
First, cumene (isopropylbenzene) is oxidised in the presence of air (\(\mathrm{O_2}\)). This aerial oxidation produces the intermediate cumene hydroperoxide. Next, cumene hydroperoxide is treated with dilute acid (\(\mathrm{H^+/H_2O}\)). Finally, acid-catalysed rearrangement and cleavage yield phenol along with acetone as a valuable by-product.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is aerial oxidation of cumene, formation of cumene hydroperoxide, treatment with dilute acid, and formation of phenol and acetone, which corresponds to 3 \(\rightarrow\) 2 \(\rightarrow\) 1 \(\rightarrow\) 4.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLSPHENOLSETHERS_MCQ_Q04 - Mechanism sequence of acid dehydration of ethanol to ethene

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps in the mechanism of acid-catalysed dehydration of ethanol to ethene at \(443\text{ K}\) in the correct order:

(1) Elimination of a proton from the carbocation to form ethene
(2) Fast protonation of ethanol to form ethyl oxonium ion
(3) Removal of ethene as it is formed to drive the equilibrium forward
(4) Slow loss of a water molecule to form the carbocation (rate-determining step)

Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Acid-catalysed dehydration of ethanol to ethene at \(443\text{ K}\) follows an \(\mathrm{E1}\)-type elimination pathway involving a protonated alcohol and a carbocation intermediate.

Step 2: Chronological Analysis
First, ethanol undergoes fast protonation by \(\mathrm{H^+}\) to form the protonated alcohol (ethyl oxonium ion). Second, the ethyl oxonium ion slowly loses a neutral water molecule to form the ethyl carbocation; this is the slowest and rate-determining step. Third, a proton is eliminated from the carbocation to form ethene and regenerate the acid catalyst. Finally, ethene is continuously removed as it is formed to shift the equilibrium to the right.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is fast protonation of ethanol, slow loss of water to form the carbocation, elimination of a proton to form ethene, and removal of ethene to drive the equilibrium, which corresponds to 2 \(\rightarrow\) 4 \(\rightarrow\) 1 \(\rightarrow\) 3.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLSPHENOLSETHERS_MCQ_Q05 - Preparation sequence of phenol from benzene via benzenesulphonic acid

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps for the preparation of phenol starting from benzene via benzenesulphonic acid in the correct order:

(1) Acidification of the sodium salt with \(\mathrm{H^+}\) to obtain phenol
(2) Sulphonation of benzene with oleum
(3) Heating benzenesulphonic acid with molten sodium hydroxide
(4) Formation of sodium phenoxide

Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Benzene is converted into phenol by introducing a sulphonic acid group followed by alkali fusion and acidification.

Step 2: Chronological Analysis
First, benzene is sulphonated using oleum (fuming sulphuric acid) to form benzenesulphonic acid. Next, benzenesulphonic acid is heated with molten sodium hydroxide (\(\mathrm{NaOH}\)). This fusion converts benzenesulphonic acid into sodium phenoxide. Finally, acidification of sodium phenoxide with \(\mathrm{H^+}\) yields phenol.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is sulphonation of benzene with oleum, heating with molten \(\mathrm{NaOH}\), formation of sodium phenoxide, and acidification to obtain phenol, which corresponds to 2 \(\rightarrow\) 3 \(\rightarrow\) 4 \(\rightarrow\) 1.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLSPHENOLSETHERS_MCQ_Q06 - Reaction sequence of ketone with Grignard reagent to tertiary alcohol

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following steps for the synthesis of a tertiary alcohol from a ketone and a Grignard reagent (\(\mathrm{R'MgX}\)) in the correct chronological sequence:

(1) Hydrolysis of the adduct with water
(2) Nucleophilic addition of the \(\mathrm{R'}\) group of the Grignard reagent to the carbonyl carbon
(3) Formation of the magnesium alkoxide adduct
(4) Liberation of the tertiary alcohol and \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)X}\)

Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Grignard reagents react with ketones via nucleophilic addition to the polar carbonyl group, followed by aqueous hydrolysis to produce tertiary alcohols.

Step 2: Chronological Analysis
First, the nucleophilic alkyl group (\(\mathrm{R'^{\delta-}}\)) of the Grignard reagent attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of the ketone. This addition produces a magnesium alkoxide adduct (\(\mathrm{R_2R'C-OMgX}\)). Next, the adduct is hydrolysed with water. Finally, hydrolysis liberates the tertiary alcohol along with \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)X}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl carbon, formation of the magnesium alkoxide adduct, hydrolysis with water, and liberation of the tertiary alcohol and \(\mathrm{Mg(OH)X}\), which corresponds to 2 \(\rightarrow\) 3 \(\rightarrow\) 1 \(\rightarrow\) 4.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLSPHENOLSETHERS_MCQ_Q07 - Bimolecular SN2 dehydration mechanism of ethanol to ethoxyethane

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following mechanistic steps for the formation of ethoxyethane from ethanol in the presence of sulphuric acid at \(413\text{ K}\) in the correct chronological order:

(1) Loss of a proton from protonated diethyl ether to yield ethoxyethane
(2) Protonation of an ethanol molecule to form ethyl oxonium ion
(3) \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) attack of a second ethanol molecule on the protonated alcohol with displacement of water
(4) Formation of protonated diethyl ether intermediate

Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
At \(413\text{ K}\), ethanol undergoes bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N2}\)) dehydration with \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) to form ethoxyethane.

Step 2: Chronological Analysis
First, one molecule of ethanol is protonated by \(\mathrm{H^+}\) to form the ethyl oxonium ion (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH_2^+}\)), converting \(-\mathrm{OH}\) into a good leaving group. Second, a second neutral ethanol molecule attacks the \(\alpha\)-carbon of the protonated alcohol via an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) pathway, displacing a water molecule. This directly forms the protonated diethyl ether intermediate (\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H-CH_2CH_3}\)). Finally, deprotonation of this intermediate yields ethoxyethane and regenerates \(\mathrm{H^+}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is protonation of ethanol, \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) attack by a second ethanol molecule with loss of water, formation of protonated diethyl ether, and loss of a proton to give ethoxyethane, which corresponds to 2 \(\rightarrow\) 3 \(\rightarrow\) 4 \(\rightarrow\) 1.

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following mechanistic steps for the reaction of 3-methylbutan-2-ol with \(\mathrm{HBr}\) to form 2-bromo-2-methylbutane in the correct chronological sequence:

(1) \(1,2\)-Hydride shift from C-3 to C-2 to form a more stable tertiary carbocation
(2) Protonation of the hydroxyl group of 3-methylbutan-2-ol
(3) Nucleophilic attack of \(\mathrm{Br^-}\) on the tertiary carbocation to form 2-bromo-2-methylbutane
(4) Loss of a water molecule to form a secondary carbocation intermediate

Choose the correct sequence from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The reaction of 3-methylbutan-2-ol with \(\mathrm{HBr}\) proceeds through an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\)-like carbocation pathway accompanied by a carbocation rearrangement to a more stable intermediate.

Step 2: Chronological Analysis
First, the hydroxyl oxygen of 3-methylbutan-2-ol is protonated by \(\mathrm{H^+}\) from \(\mathrm{HBr}\) to form a good leaving group (\(-\mathrm{OH_2^+}\)). Second, departure of a water molecule generates a secondary carbocation at C-2. Third, because a tertiary carbocation is more stable than a secondary one, a \(1,2\)-hydride shift occurs from C-3 to C-2 to give the tertiary carbocation. Finally, the bromide ion (\(\mathrm{Br^-}\)) attacks this tertiary carbocation to yield 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct sequence is protonation of the hydroxyl group, loss of water to form a secondary carbocation, \(1,2\)-hydride shift to form a tertiary carbocation, and nucleophilic attack of \(\mathrm{Br^-}\), which corresponds to 2 \(\rightarrow\) 4 \(\rightarrow\) 1 \(\rightarrow\) 3.
